emails.subject: You are not bad with money
emails.preview: Four reasons you have been avoiding the books.
body: Let me clear something out of the way first, because it will block everything else I send you.
You have been avoiding your financial statements.
There is a file you close faster than you open it. You know the one.
Most owners explain that to themselves with character. Discipline. Being bad with the money stuff.
After thirty-five years of opening other people's books, I can tell you the explanation is structural.
There are four reasons, and I have never met an owner who did not have at least two of them.
One. Your reports were built for your tax preparer.
They are organized around what the IRS needs to know.
You open one looking for something that helps you decide on a Tuesday. You find nothing that speaks to it. You close the file.
That is a design problem in the report.
Two. Nobody has reviewed your chart of accounts since QuickBooks was set up.
Categories go stale. Expenses get parked in miscellaneous because nobody knows where else to put them.
Miscellaneous is not a category. It is a confession.
Three. Nobody ever taught you to read a balance sheet.
You were never supposed to arrive at this already knowing.
You are untrained. Untrained is fixable in an afternoon.
Four, and this is the honest one. Every previous attempt cost you time and gave you back confusion.
So avoidance became the rational move.
Read that fourth one again.
Your avoidance has been working correctly. It is a sensible response to a process that has never once paid you back.
None of the four are personal failings. All four are fixable.
So before you read another chapter, do the smallest possible version of looking.
Three questions, about two minutes. Best estimates are fine on every one of them. You will not need to open anything.
It shows you the gap between what your business looks like it keeps and what it actually keeps.

emails.subject: Nobody was ever hired to stand there
emails.preview: The most expensive gap in small business.
body: A profitable owner came to me for tax planning. Routine work.
She had a bookkeeper. She had a CPA. Both were competent and both were doing precisely what they were hired to do.
We surfaced roughly twenty thousand dollars in savings for that year, with more built into the structure going forward.
Nobody had missed it through carelessness.
It survived because of where it was sitting.
Here is the shape of your financial life, and almost every owner's.
Somebody records your transactions. That is bookkeeping. It answers one question, which is whether the math added up.
Somebody files your return. That is tax preparation. It looks backward at a year that already closed.
Between those two jobs is a space where the actual decisions live.
What should we do next.
Nobody is standing in that space.
Your people are good. It was simply never anybody's job.
I call it the Missing Middle, and I think it is the most expensive gap in small business.
It is where the overpaid sales tax sits.
It is where the misclassified expense sits, quietly making your marketing look more expensive than it is.
It is where the price you have not raised in three years sits.
Your books are honest. They have been answering somebody else's questions for years, which is a different problem entirely.
Chapter 1 shows you how wide that gap has grown in your business.
Thirty minutes, and you already have everything you need to do it.

emails.subject: A question, and no pitch
emails.preview: Something I would like to know about you.
body: I have asked every new client the same question for about fifteen years.
It is never about revenue and it is never about software.
I ask what made them call.
The answers are almost always specific, and almost always recent.
A banker asked for twelve months of financials and the file that came back was embarrassing.
A tax bill arrived that was several thousand dollars more than expected, and there was no way to check whether it was right.
A partner asked a simple question over dinner and got a vague answer.
Payroll week came and the number in the account did not quite cover what was owed.
Nobody wakes up wanting to look at their books.
Something makes them look.
So let me ask you, {{contact.first_name}}.

One line is plenty. Whatever came to mind in the first two seconds is usually the honest answer.

emails.subject: He had already signed the lease
emails.preview: The appointment that decided what I do.
body: A few years ago a restaurant owner named Alberto came to see me.
Spanish food, his grandmother's recipes from Puerto Rico. The place was always busy.
He knew what I did for a living. He booked an appointment to talk about opening a second location near a train station.
I asked him one question.
Do you feel the first restaurant is strong enough to sustain a second one?
He paused.
Then he said, it's too late. I've already signed the lease.
He had not come for advice. He had come for support of a decision that was already made.
Six months later he lost both businesses.
I think about that appointment more than any other in my career.
Alberto was a good operator. The food was excellent and the room was full every night.
What he was missing was the difference between a decision made on feeling and a decision made on numbers.
Nobody had ever shown it to him.
He was making the same kind of call an executive team makes, with none of the financial work that normally sits underneath it.
That was the appointment where I understood what small business owners are actually up against.
You have somebody recording what happened. You have somebody filing a return about a year that already closed.
Between them is the room where the decision gets made, and it is empty.
I have spent every year since standing in that room.
The point of it is plain enough. When an owner is six weeks out from signing a lease, somebody should be able to tell her what her own numbers say about it.
Alberto did not have that person.
Most owners do not.
That is why I wrote the book down.
Jackie

emails.subject: She could not prove it was good
emails.preview: Twelve percent up, twenty percent down.
body: She went to her bank for a line of credit.
Revenue was up twelve percent on the year. She felt fine walking in.
She brought what she had. A P&L from two quarters back. A balance sheet her bookkeeper had generated that she could not explain. No cash flow statement.
The banker was polite. He asked a few questions.
Her answers sounded vague even to her own ears.
Then he asked the one she remembers.
Your revenue is up twelve percent and your cash position has dropped twenty percent. Can you explain the gap?
She could not. She had no idea.
She walked out with nothing.
Here is the part of that story that has stayed with me for years.
Her business was fine.
She could not prove it was fine, and to a bank those two things are the same thing.
She was not angry at the banker afterward. She was angry at herself, which is worse and lasts longer.
Eighteen months later she walked back into the same building.
Twelve-month rolling P&L. A balance sheet she could explain line by line. A cash flow statement that tied exactly to her bank account. A one page narrative she had written herself.
The banker asked hard questions again and she answered every one out of her books.
The business got funded.
She was not louder the second time. She was quieter.
If you are reading this with a specific meeting somewhere ahead of you, a bank, a partner, a buyer, then you already know what your file looks like today.
The fastest way to find out what it is missing is to let somebody read it who is not you.

emails.subject: She waited a year
emails.preview: What the first month turned up.
body: Becky runs an event meeting space here in Las Vegas.
She knew her books needed attention for more than a year before she called me.
She told me later what had held her there. She was afraid the switch would be grueling, and she was afraid of what a cleanup would turn up.
That is the most common reason owners wait, and almost nobody says it out loud.
In the first month we found ten errors from her previous bookkeeper.
Ten. In one month. In the accounts of a business that looked completely fine from the outside.
Here is the part I want you to notice.
Becky did not get angry when she saw the list.
She was relieved.
For a year she had been carrying a vague heavy sense that something was off, with nothing she could point at.
Now she had specific entries, specific dates, specific amounts.
A list is workable. A suspicion is not.
Her words afterward were simple, efficient and stress-free, which is a strange set of adjectives for the thing she had spent a year dreading.
And the year she spent waiting was the expensive part. The errors were running the whole time.
Whatever you suspect about your own books is either true or it is not.
Both of those answers are better than the suspicion.

emails.preview: Five reasons owners stall. Send me a number.
body: No pitch today. I want to ask you something and I would like a real answer.

Two. You are afraid of what you will find.
You have a sense of what is in there and you are not sure you want it confirmed this month.

Four. You have tried before and watched it slide back.
You brought somebody in, or you set something up, and within a quarter it was the same again. Now you are careful about trying a third time.
Five. Money is genuinely tight right now.
The real version of that, where payroll is a live decision every single month.
All five are legitimate. I have sat across from owners in every one of them.

emails.subject: A quiet Tuesday
emails.preview: What it looks like when the books stop running you.
body: Happy {{right_now.day}}.
I want to tell you about Norma. She runs the financial administration for a private school in New Jersey.
When we started, she was drowning in paper.
Every month she printed reports, typed numbers into Excel, and reconciled the accounts by hand. It consumed hours of her week and every bit of it ran through her.
If Norma got sick, the financials stopped. If Norma took vacation, nothing moved.
She was not running the books. The books were running her.
We moved the school onto an automated setup and I trained the team. The reporting maintains itself now.
Here is what changed, and it is quieter than you would expect.
On a Tuesday morning she opens one report. Three minutes.
She knows where the cash sits, what came in, what went out, and whether anything moved that should not have.
Then she closes it and goes and does her actual job.
Nobody is waiting on her for a number. Nothing is being rebuilt from scratch. The month does not depend on her remembering.
She took a vacation and the reports still went out.
There is no dramatic version of this story, which is exactly what makes it worth having.
An ordinary weekday where the numbers are simply there is the whole prize.
You still do the work. You stop being the only route to the answer.

emails.subject: The shoebox weekend
emails.preview: Why it stopped by Sunday night.
body: There is a version of this you have already tried.
Maybe a weekend with a box of receipts. Maybe software you bought and stopped opening. Maybe a book like this one you meant to finish.
It stopped somewhere around Sunday night, and you have quietly held it against yourself ever since.
I have watched too many hard working owners do this to believe it is about discipline.
Here is what actually happens.
You open the books and you see everything at once.
The categories that are wrong. The subscription nobody canceled. The price you have not raised. The invoice from March that never got chased.
All of it, in one sitting.
So you try to fix all of it, in one sitting.
By hour three you are underwater, and by Sunday night you have stopped.
That is why the framework is sequenced.
Chapter 1 asks you to look. Only look. You fix nothing.
The fixing comes in Chapter 4, and by then you know what is worth fixing and in what order.
Owners who cut before they have finished finding always cut the wrong things. They cancel the subscription that was generating revenue and keep the one that was not.
Thirty minutes of looking is reachable. You can hold that on a Tuesday.
And something shifts after the first step. The second one stops looking like a mountain.
That surprises almost everybody.

emails.subject: QuickBooks was never the problem
emails.preview: The thing everyone blames, and why it is innocent.
body: Let me get in front of something.
When an owner decides to fix her finances, the first move is almost always software.
New subscription. Fresh setup. A weekend importing everything.
Then six months later, the same fog.
I want to defend the software here, because it usually takes the blame unfairly.
QuickBooks is a platform. It does what it was built to do and it does it well.
The system is how you use it.
The categories you set up. The reports you actually run. The integrations you connect. The person who maintains it and what you have asked them to look for.
A tool with no system underneath it produces tidy records and no answers.
So you end up with a subscription, a clean looking dashboard, and the same question you started with.
Are we making money, or does it just look that way.
Here is my honest position on your books.
They are probably fine as a record.
They were built to answer what the IRS needs to know, and they answer it correctly.
The gap is that nobody has ever asked them the questions you need answered before Monday.
That is a reading problem, and no amount of software solves a reading problem.
Chapter 5 covers what to build so the answers arrive without you assembling them.
Before that, Chapter 3 teaches you to read the three statements you already own as one system.
You have the tools. Nobody has shown you where to look.
Jackie

emails.subject: More revenue will not save you
emails.preview: How a profitable business runs out of money.
body: Every owner reaches for the same lever.
More jobs. More marketing. Another salesperson.
It feels like progress and it is the obvious move.
Then you run into the arithmetic in Chapter 3, and it changes how you think about the whole year.
A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of money.
Profit is what your P&L says you earned. Cash is what your bank account says you have.
They are two different numbers and they move at different times.
You invoice in March. You get paid in June.
The P&L celebrates in March. The bank account waits until June.
Meanwhile payroll ran in April and again in May.
That gap is where good businesses die, and adding revenue makes it wider.
More work means more bought up front, more hours paid before anyone pays you, and more invoices sitting out there unpaid.
Growth does not fix this. Growth exposes it.
So here is a question you can answer standing up, in about ten seconds, from memory.
Over the last year, did the money in your bank account move in the same direction as the profit on your P&L?
Most owners cannot answer that with any confidence, and that is the entire point.
You do not need exact figures today. You need to know the question exists, and to notice that nobody has ever asked it of your business.
The two minute version of the answer is here, and your best estimate is fine.

emails.subject: Three kinds of owner
emails.preview: One of these describes your week exactly.
body: Happy {{right_now.day}}.
Short diagnostic today. Every owner I meet is standing in one of three places.
One. Reactive.
Your week sets your priorities. You find out about a problem when it becomes a problem.
The tax bill is a surprise. The slow month is a surprise.
You perform confidence at networking events and do the real arithmetic alone at two in the morning.
Two. Informed.
You look at the numbers. You have a rough sense of the shape of things.
You still could not tell a banker why revenue is up and cash is down.
You still could not say which job in your business actually makes money.
You have information. You do not have a position.
Three. In command.
You open one report on a Monday and you know where you stand.
You make pricing decisions from numbers rather than nerve.
When somebody asks a hard question, you say let me show you in my books, and then you do.
The composure is real, because there is something underneath it.
Most owners reading this are in one. A decent number are in two.
Almost nobody arrives at three by accident.
Getting from one to two is looking.
Getting from two to three is sequence, which is most of what the book is about.
If you are in one, that is where nearly everybody starts, including most of my clients on the day they first called me.
Read the three again and be honest about which one describes yesterday.
You cannot fix the wrong problem into the right result.

emails.subject: Two ways to spend a year
emails.preview: Both take twelve months. One arrives somewhere.
body: There are two ways to spend the next twelve months.
Path one. Everything stays as it is.
The statements keep arriving and you keep meaning to look properly.
Tax time keeps producing surprises.
You keep pricing from instinct.
Revenue moves a little. Some months are good. The shape of the year never changes.
Next year you are twelve months older, running the same week, holding the same question you are holding now.
And whatever has been leaking has had another year to leak.
Path two. You take the first step, and then the next one.
Thirty minutes of looking.
Then following the money until the suspicion becomes a list.
Then reading your three statements as one thing.
Then cutting, in order.
One step at a time, in the sequence that works.
Twelve months later you know where you stand. You walk into a bank prepared. You price from numbers.
The same twelve months either way.
Path one costs you the year and hands you back the same business.
Path two costs you focused attention on unglamorous work you have been avoiding.
I am not asking you to choose today.
Just notice that you are standing at a fork, and that standing still quietly picks path one.
Jackie
Jacqueline A. Oberst, MS, CEPA
Sunderland Valley Enterprises

Right now, for most owners, the answer gets decided by whatever their numbers happen to be able to prove on the day somebody asks.
That is the difference between running and running somewhere.
It is also the difference between hoping the people counting on you are safe and knowing it.
Growth ready. Loan ready. Sale ready.

I will be honest about what usually happens next.
Most people read the introduction, agree with all of it, and put it down.
That is fine. I have done it with better books than mine.
Here is the only part I would push back on.
The business does not sit still while the book does.
The categories stay wrong. The subscription keeps running. The price stays where it was.
A year of that is not nothing.
